title: Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Clinical Time-Series Models
claim: A frozen model's representations are mapped onto a time-variable grid and decomposed into reusable, interpretable concepts that drive predictions and explanations.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, top flow bar with SAE, grid and dictionary entry below
description: A wide diagram with a top row of pastel boxes running left to right: EHR Event Sequence (with small event chips), Backbone, Prediction Head, LLM Verbalizer, then Natural Language Explanation. Blue, green and orange arrows, some dashed, branch down from the backbone. The lower left panel is a cream rounded box. In it a vertical stack runs H[B,L,D], then H_grid[B,T,V,D], then a TI-SAE block, then reconstructed H_grid, with a reconstruction loss loop on the side. The center panel is a time (48h) by variables grid with blue dots. Colored Gaussian curves with mu and sigma labels and shaded boxes labeled k=42, 105 and 7 mark the temporal islands. The right panel is an orange Dictionary Entry card (k=42) with variable-composition bars for serum creatinine, urine output and BUN, and a temporal island curve labeled 'Acute Renal Function Decline'. A Prediction Selector box links it to the verbalizer.
caption: \textbf{Overview of the Temporal Island SAE (\tisae{}).} A frozen backbone transforms an EHR event sequence into a hidden representation $H[B,L,D]$, which is then scattered into a dense representation grid $\Hgrid[B,T,V,D]$. \tisae{} learns a dictionary of $K$ latents, each with $M$ temporal Gaussian islands (colored curves) defining when the concept is active, and sparse variable-composition weights $w_k$ defining which variables are involved. Each island corresponds to an interpretable clinical concept with explicit temporal extent and variable structure.
abstract: Deep learning models for electronic health records achieve strong predictive performance but provide little insight into what clinical concepts they represent internally. Post-hoc attribution methods produce per-cell importance scores that lack temporal coherence, cross-variable structure, and reusability across patients. We introduce the Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoder (TI-SAE), which learns a backbone-specific, patient-shared clinical concept dictionary from a frozen predictive model's representations. Each dictionary entry (latent) is defined by learned temporal Gaussian islands (specifying when the concept is active) and a sparse variable-composition vector (specifying which variables are involved). A decoupled selector then identifies which dictionary entries drive each patient's prediction, separating representation learning from attribution. We evaluate TI-SAE across five backbone architectures spanning different representation strategies on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (three prediction tasks each). TI-SAE produces structured clinical concepts that go beyond transient attribution heatmaps while achieving strong performance on standard faithfulness benchmarks.
